title_en: Hong Kong Baiyue Financial Services Co., Ltd. v. Hong Kong Hongli Gourmet Co., Ltd. — dispute over payment for goods
keywords_en: civil; loan contract dispute; first instance; intermediate people's court; Guangdong Province; Hong Kong Special Administrative Region; legal person; General Principles of Civil Law; Regulations on Loan Contracts; jurisdiction; application of law; validity of loan agreement; legality of interest rate, compound interest, and penalty interest; support plaintiff; loan agreement; Hong Kong company; joint venture hotel; overdue repayment; arbitration; Hongli Gourmet Co., Ltd. goods payment dispute
full_text_en:
Hong Kong Baiyue Financial Services Ltd. v. Hong Kong Hongli Gourmet Food Ltd. — Loan Dispute

Plaintiff: Hong Kong Baiyue Financial Services Ltd.

Legal Representative: Cai Jinghua, Executive Director and Deputy General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Liu Xianzhang, Deputy Manager of the Credit Department.

Agent ad litem: Su Zuyao, Lawyer of Guangdong Foreign Economic Law Firm.

Defendant: Hong Kong Hongli Gourmet Food Ltd.

Legal Representative: Lin Xian, Director and General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Liang Ziyun, former Accountant of Guangzhou Hualigong Hotel.

The plaintiff, Hong Kong Baiyue Financial Services Ltd., filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province regarding a loan agreement dispute with the defendant, Hong Kong Hongli Gourmet Food Ltd.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The defendant invested in a cooperative venture in Guangzhou, the Guangzhou Hualigong Hotel, and requested a Hong Kong dollar loan from the plaintiff. In September 1986, the plaintiff and the defendant signed a loan agreement in Hong Kong, stipulating that the plaintiff would lend HKD 7,800,000 to the defendant, repayable in 9 installments of principal and interest over five years. After the plaintiff fully disbursed the loan in accordance with the agreement, the defendant has only repaid interest of HKD 169,537.39, and the overdue principal and interest have exceeded HKD 10,000,000. The plaintiff requests the court, in accordance with the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China and relevant Chinese laws, to order the defendant to repay the loan principal of HKD 7,800,000, plus loan interest and penalty interest of HKD 5,007,895.6 as of April 30, 1991, and to compensate the plaintiff for litigation costs of HKD 73,760, notarization fees of HKD 1,585, and attorney fees of RMB 11,000.

Defendant's Defense: The loan from the plaintiff has been invested in the Guangzhou Hualigong Hotel. In the initial period after the hotel opened, it operated at a loss, and the defendant repaid loan interest of HKD 169,537.39. When the hotel turned profitable in the second half of 1988, a dispute arose with the Chinese partner, making it impossible to repay principal and interest as agreed. The dispute between the defendant and the hotel's Chinese partner is currently under arbitration at the Shenzhen Sub-Commission of the China International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission. After the Chinese partner compensates for the losses, the defendant will repay the loan. The defendant requests the plaintiff to reduce or waive the calculation of interest, compound interest, and penalty interest.

Facts Found by the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court:

In March 1986, the defendant, Hong Kong Hongli Gourmet Food Ltd., signed a contract with Guangzhou Shijing Commercial Service Company for a cooperative venture to operate the Guangzhou Hualigong Hotel. On September 5, 1986, to raise funds, the defendant signed a loan agreement with the plaintiff, Baiyue Financial Services Ltd. The contract stipulated: 1. The plaintiff would lend HKD 7,800,000 to the defendant; 2. The loan term was 5 years; 3. The defendant would repay principal and interest in 9 installments over 5 years, with the first installment due on the same date one year after the first drawdown, and thereafter every six months, each installment being 1/9 of the total loan plus interest; 4. Interest would be calculated on a 365-day year basis, payable at the end of each month, with unpaid interest automatically converted into principal and compounded, plus penalty interest at 20% of the overdue interest; 5. The interest rate would be the Hong Kong dollar prime rate of the Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch plus 1%; 6. The plaintiff would charge an arrangement fee of 0.5% of the total loan amount; 7. The loan agreement would be governed by Hong Kong law and the laws of the People's Republic of China. After the contract was concluded, the plaintiff collected an arrangement fee of HKD 39,000 from the defendant. The defendant drew HKD 2,500,000 on September 8, 1986, HKD 2,000,000 on September 15, and HKD 3,300,000 on September 27, totaling HKD 7,800,000. On October 2 and December 10 of the same year, and on February 27, 1987, the defendant repaid interest totaling HKD 169,537.39. As of April 30, 1991, the defendant owed the plaintiff past-due principal of HKD 6,066,666.67, interest and compound interest of HKD 4,173,246.33, and penalty interest of HKD 834,649.27. After repeated unsuccessful demands, the plaintiff filed suit with the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court. The plaintiff incurred notarization fees for evidence of HKD 1,585 and attorney fees of RMB 11,000 for this lawsuit.

The contractual dispute between the defendant and its partner in the cooperative venture to operate the Guangzhou Hualigong Hotel is currently under arbitration at the Shenzhen Sub-Commission of the China International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission.

Opinion of the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court:

1. Regarding jurisdiction. The plaintiff and defendant are both Hong Kong enterprise legal persons. The loan agreement was signed and performed in Hong Kong, and the parties did not have a written agreement to submit to the jurisdiction of a court of the People's Republic of China. By reference to Article 244 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this case would not normally fall under the jurisdiction of a court of the People's Republic of China. However, the plaintiff insisted on filing suit in the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court on the grounds that the defendant's loan was invested in a cooperative enterprise in Guangzhou, and the defendant did not object to the jurisdiction and responded to the lawsuit. By reference to Article 245 of the Civil Procedure Law, the defendant is deemed to have accepted the jurisdiction of the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court.

2. Regarding the applicable law. The plaintiff and defendant agreed that the handling of disputes under the loan contract would be governed by Hong Kong law and the laws of the People's Republic of China. During the litigation, the plaintiff and defendant, after further consultation, agreed to choose the laws of the People's Republic of China. By reference to Article 145(1) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the substantive law of the People's Republic of China is chosen as the governing law for this case.

3. Regarding the binding force of the loan agreement. Upon examination, the loan agreement in this case is valid: the parties have legal capacity; their intent is genuine; the form of the agreement meets legal requirements. The only issue is whether the rights and obligations stipulated in the contract—specifically, the agreed interest rate, compound interest, penalty interest, and arrangement fee—conflict with the laws and policies of the People's Republic of China. Upon examination: (1) The plaintiff and defendant agreed that the loan interest rate would be the Hong Kong dollar prime rate of the Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch plus 1%. According to investigation, the Hong Kong dollar prime rate of the Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch is the rate published by the Hong Kong Association of Banks. Pursuant to relevant State Council regulations, interest rates for foreign currency loans shall be implemented according to the comprehensive rate formulated by the Head Office of the Bank of China; alternatively, the lending and borrowing parties may negotiate and determine the rate based on international market interest rates, or determine the rate by adding a certain spread to the agreed rate. The plaintiff is a financial company registered in Hong Kong, and under relevant Hong Kong financial management regulations, its deposit and loan interest rates may be higher than bank rates. Therefore, the interest rate agreed upon by the plaintiff and defendant is confirmed to be legal in that locality. At the same time, China permits non-bank financial institutions to charge slightly higher interest rates for investment loans than bank loan rates. Thus, the interest rate agreed upon by the plaintiff and defendant does not conflict with China's relevant laws and regulations and should be valid. (2) The plaintiff and defendant agreed that unpaid interest under the agreement would be automatically converted into principal and compounded. The Interim Provisions on Interest Rate Management promulgated by the People's Bank of China stipulate: "Financial institutions shall settle interest quarterly on working capital loans and technological transformation loans to enterprises... interest that cannot be paid may be compounded." The Industrial and Commercial Bank of China's Interim Measures on Foreign Exchange Loans stipulate: "If a borrowing unit fails to pay interest on time, the bank shall automatically transfer the overdue interest into principal and compound it." Therefore, the agreement on compound interest between the plaintiff and defendant is permitted by China's laws and regulations and should be valid. (3) The plaintiff and defendant agreed that unpaid interest under the agreement, in addition to being converted into principal and compounded, would incur penalty interest at 20% of the overdue interest. Penalty interest is an additional charge on interest for default by the borrower in exceeding the repayment period, misappropriating loans, or other breaches. Article 16 of the Loan Contract Regulations promulgated by the State Council stipulates: "If the borrowing party fails to repay the loan on schedule, the lending party has the right... to charge penalty interest in accordance with bank regulations." Penalty interest in China's credit relations is directed at the outstanding loan principal; in this case, the penalty interest is directed at the overdue interest portion. The loan in this case is relatively fair and favorable. Therefore, the agreement on penalty interest between the plaintiff and defendant does not violate the laws and regulations of the People's Republic of China, and its binding effect should be recognized. (4) The plaintiff and defendant agreed that the plaintiff would charge an arrangement fee (i.e., handling fee) of 0.5% of the total loan amount. In mainland China's credit relations, there is no practice of charging arrangement fees. However, this is common practice in international credit. This case involves a Hong Kong foreign currency loan, and both parties are Hong Kong companies; international practice should be followed. Therefore, this stipulation is deemed binding. Based on the above findings, the loan agreement signed between the plaintiff and defendant is protected by law by reference to Article 90 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China. The contract is legally binding on both parties. The defendant's failure to repay principal and interest on time constitutes a breach of contract. By reference to Article 16 of the Loan Contract Regulations, the lending party has the right to demand recovery of the loan within a specified period and to require payment of compound interest and penalty interest in accordance with the agreement. The plaintiff's request to recover the principal that has not yet fallen due on the grounds of the defendant's breach is legally justified and should be supported. The plaintiff's request that the defendant bear the attorney fees incurred is not a necessary litigation expense and is not recognized. The defendant's request to repay the loan only after the arbitration award in the cooperative venture contract dispute, and to reduce or waive interest, compound interest, and penalty interest, is not supported.

Accordingly, the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court, on May 31, 1991, rendered the following judgment:

1. The defendant shall, within 30 days from the day following the effective date of this judgment, repay to the plaintiff the principal of HKD 7,800,000 plus interest (interest calculated from May 1, 1991, until the date of full payment, at the Hong Kong dollar prime rate of the Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch plus 1%). For overdue payment, compound interest and penalty interest shall be calculated in accordance with the terms of the loan agreement.

2. The defendant shall, within 30 days from the day following the effective date of this judgment, pay to the plaintiff interest of HKD 4,173,246.33 and penalty interest of HKD 834,649.27, plus compound interest on the interest (compound interest calculated from May 1, 1991, until the date of full payment, at the Hong Kong dollar prime rate of the Bank of China, Hong Kong Branch plus 1%).

3. The defendant shall, within 10 days from the day following the effective date of this judgment, compensate the plaintiff for the notarization fees for evidence of HKD 1,585.

4. All other claims of the plaintiff and the defendant are dismissed.

Court costs of this case in the amount of RMB (foreign exchange certificate) 48,433.6 shall be borne by the defendant.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, neither the plaintiff nor the defendant appealed.
